---
title: "The regression t statistic"
execute:
  enabled: true

---

The fitted Provo slope is positive. But the observed slope would change if we
could repeat the sampling process. How large is the estimate relative to the
sampling variation expected when the population slope has a particular value?
The **coefficient $t$ statistic** answers that question by measuring the distance
between an estimate and a hypothesized coefficient in estimated standard error
units.

Recall that a [null hypothesis](../statistical-inference/null-hypotheses-and-test-statistics.qmd)
specifies the value used to derive the reference distribution of a test
statistic. We will use $H_0:\beta_1=0$, where $\beta_1$ is the population slope
for modeled cloze surprisal. We first derive the sampling variance of the slope,
then replace the unknown response variance with the residual estimate, and
finally calculate the resulting statistic from the Provo observations.

## Deriving the slope standard error

Suppose that the responses follow the Gaussian linear model

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

The abbreviation **iid** means independent and identically distributed. Thus
the model assigns each error a Gaussian distribution with mean zero and common
variance $\sigma^2$, and it treats distinct errors as independent. These
assumptions give the exact finite sample reference distribution derived below.

The OLS slope from [least squares](frequentist-linear-regression.qmd#from-discrepancies-to-an-objective)
is

$$
\widehat\beta_1
=
\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)(Y_i-\overline Y)}
{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2}.
$$

Let

$$
S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2.
$$

Substitute $Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i$ into the slope formula. The
constant intercept disappears after centering, and the centered predictor
multiplied by $\beta_1$ contributes $\beta_1S_{xx}$. We therefore obtain

$$
\widehat\beta_1
=
\beta_1
+
\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)\varepsilon_i}{S_{xx}}.
$$

This equation isolates the sampling error in the slope. Because the errors are
independent and each has variance $\sigma^2$, the variance of their weighted sum
is the sum of the weighted variances:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat\beta_1\mid\mathbf x]
&=
\frac{
\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2\sigma^2
}{S_{xx}^2} \\
&=
\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

If $\sigma$ were known, dividing $\widehat\beta_1-\beta_1$ by
$\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}$ would produce a standard normal random variable. We do
not know $\sigma$. The [residual standard error](residuals.qmd#residual-standard-error)

$$
s=\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-2}}
$$

estimates it. The corresponding **standard error of the slope** is

$$
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\beta_1)
=
\frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}.
$$

Why does replacing $\sigma$ produce a $t$ distribution? Standardize each error
as $z_i=\varepsilon_i/\sigma$ and define

$$
u_i=\frac{x_i-\overline x}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}.
$$

The [projection geometry](design-matrices.qmd#projection-as-fitted-plus-residual)
gives a useful way to read this equation. A **direction** is a vector that points
along one axis of possible variation, and a **component** is the amount of
another vector pointing along that direction. Because $\sum_i u_i^2=1$, the
vector $\mathbf u$ has length one and is called a **unit direction**. The
standardized slope error is the component of the Gaussian error vector in the
$\mathbf u$ direction:

$$
\frac{\widehat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}
=
\sum_i u_i z_i.
$$

Fitting the intercept and slope removes two directions from the error vector:
the constant direction and the centered predictor direction $\mathbf u$. The
residuals occupy the remaining $n-2$ perpendicular directions. A Gaussian error
vector with covariance $\sigma^2\mathbf I$ has independent standard normal
components along perpendicular unit directions. Thus the slope component is
independent of the residual components, while the sum of the $n-2$ squared
residual components has a [chi-squared distribution](../random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd).
Specifically,

$$
\frac{(n-2)s^2}{\sigma^2}
\sim
\chi^2_{n-2}.
$$

A standard normal component divided by the square root of an independent
chi-squared random variable divided by its degrees of freedom has a
[Student $t$ distribution](../random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution.qmd).
Thus, under $H_0:\beta_1=\beta_{1,0}$,

$$
T
=
\frac{
\widehat\beta_1-\beta_{1,0}
}{
s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}
}
\sim
t_{n-2}.
$$

The null value for the usual `lm()` output is $\beta_{1,0}=0$.

## Calculating the Provo t statistic

```{r}
#| label: calculate-provo-regression-t
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits,
  data = provo
)

x <- provo$cloze_surprisal_bits
sxx <- sum((x - mean(x))^2)
sse <- sum(residuals(fit)^2)
residual_df <- nrow(provo) - length(coef(fit))
residual_standard_error <- sqrt(sse / residual_df)
slope_estimate <- coef(fit)[["cloze_surprisal_bits"]]
slope_standard_error <- residual_standard_error / sqrt(sxx)
null_slope <- 0
t_observed <-
  (slope_estimate - null_slope) / slope_standard_error
two_sided_p_value <-
  2 * pt(-abs(t_observed), df = residual_df)

lm_slope_output <- coef(summary(fit))["cloze_surprisal_bits", ]
stopifnot(
  abs(slope_standard_error - lm_slope_output[["Std. Error"]]) < 1e-12,
  abs(t_observed - lm_slope_output[["t value"]]) < 1e-12,
  abs(two_sided_p_value - lm_slope_output[["Pr(>|t|)"]]) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(
  slope_estimate = slope_estimate,
  residual_standard_error = residual_standard_error,
  sxx = sxx,
  slope_standard_error = slope_standard_error,
  null_slope = null_slope,
  t_statistic = t_observed,
  residual_degrees_of_freedom = residual_df,
  two_sided_p_value = two_sided_p_value
)
```

The direct calculation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\beta_1)
&=
\frac{`r format(residual_standard_error, digits = 7)`}
{\sqrt{`r format(sxx, digits = 7)`}} \\
&=
`r format(slope_standard_error, digits = 7)`, \\
T
&=
\frac{`r format(slope_estimate, digits = 7)`-0}
{`r format(slope_standard_error, digits = 7)`} \\
&=
`r format(t_observed, digits = 7)`.
\end{aligned}
$$

This value matches the `t value` in `summary(fit)`. The calculation also shows
what that output means: the estimated Provo slope lies about
`r sprintf("%.2f", abs(t_observed))` estimated OLS standard errors from the null
value zero.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-data-for-t
#| fig-cap: "Observed Provo position summaries and the fitted line whose slope enters the t statistic."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 160L)
)
grid$fitted <- predict(fit, newdata = grid)
point_opacity <- 0.22

ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = fitted),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Reading the reference distribution

The two-sided $p$ value adds the probability, under the null model, of obtaining
a $t$ statistic at least as far from zero in either direction:

$$
p
=
\mathbb{P}_{H_0}
\left(
|T|\geq |t_{\mathrm{obs}}|
\right).
$$

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-t-reference
#| fig-cap: "Two-sided tail probability under a zero Provo slope. The point marks the statistic and p value calculated from the observed data."
t_tail_grid <- data.frame(
  absolute_t = seq(0, abs(t_observed) * 1.08, length.out = 2001L)
)
t_tail_grid$two_sided_probability <-
  2 * pt(-t_tail_grid$absolute_t, df = residual_df)

ggplot(t_tail_grid, aes(absolute_t, two_sided_probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = abs(t_observed),
    color = "#B4473A",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(
      absolute_t = abs(t_observed),
      two_sided_probability = two_sided_p_value
    ),
    color = "#B4473A",
    size = 2
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Absolute t statistic", y = "Two-sided tail probability (log scale)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

For these data, the two-sided value is
`r format(two_sided_p_value, scientific = TRUE, digits = 4)`. Under repeated
samples from the null model, this is the probability of obtaining a statistic
at least this extreme. The probability that the null hypothesis is true is a
different quantity.

The exact $t$ reference calculation treats the Provo position rows as
independent Gaussian observations with a common conditional variance. Positions
from the same passage may remain dependent. The [clustered sensitivity
calculation](linear-regression-uncertainty.qmd#conventional-ols-uncertainty)
changes the estimated coefficient variance to retain passage grouping. That
change also changes the appropriate reference calculation.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why does greater spread in $x$ reduce the conventional slope standard error?
2. Where does the $n-2$ degrees of freedom come from?
3. What does the numerator of the $t$ statistic measure?
4. Which assumptions give the exact Student $t$ reference distribution?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. A larger $S_{xx}$ provides more information about how the conditional mean changes across predictor values, and the standard error divides by $\sqrt{S_{xx}}$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The simple regression estimates two coefficients, an intercept and a slope, leaving $n-2$ residual degrees of freedom. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. It measures the distance between the estimated slope and the slope specified by the null hypothesis. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Independent Gaussian errors with mean zero and a common conditional variance give the exact finite sample result. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
